Review 1.1

Comprehensive functional characterization of cancer-testis antigens defines obligate participation in multiple hallmarks of cancer. Maxfield KE, Taus PJ, Corcoran K, Wooten J, Macion J, Zhou Y, Borromeo M, Kollipara RK, Yan J, Xie Y, Xie XJ, Whitehurst AW. Nat Commun. 2015 Nov 16;6:8840. doi: 10.1038/ncomms9840. PMID: 26567849

Review 2.2

Figure 2B: can the authors double check the upset plot? It seems that the numbers for the CTexploreR list do not add up to 146, but I might be mistaken.

I’ve checked that using the upset plot with the numbers, that is in the 02 rmd on the paper repo. Indeed, summing all the numbers above the bars make 146 : 48+19+7+4+14+10+8+2+1+12+4+2+1+7+2+1+1+3

Review 2.4-3.1

2.4 Non-Methdep CG genes do not seem to be regulated by DNA methylation. What are the hypotheses for their regulation? Chromatin marks or maybe downstream transcriptional targets of other Methdep CG genes? Potential mechanisms should be discussed in more details in the discussion.

3.1 It is unclear at this stage what differentiates Methdep from non-Methdep CG genes. Beside their enrichment on the X-chromosome, are there other features that distinguish the Methdep from non-Methdep CG genes ? It would be valuable to correlate with the presence or not of a CpG island at the promoter (or compare promoter CG richness), as this is the type of promoters that is typically methylation-sensitive. Also, transcription factor binding sites ?

Both the reviewers wanted us to characterise the regulation of the CG Non-Methdep. Charles and Axelle are going to have a look at transcription factors.

I’m going to focus on the CpG density : compare MethDep and Non-MethDep promoters.

In CTexploreR, we characterised promoter as 1000nt upstream TSS and 200 nt downstream TSS. There’s a column CpG_density, that gives the density of CpG within each promoter (number of CpG / promoter length * 100), and a column CpG_promoter, that classifies the promoters according to their CpG densities: “low” (CpG_density < 2), “intermediate” (CpG_density >= 2 & CpG_density < 4), and “high” (CpG_density >= 4). I will be using that?

methdepCT <- CT_genes %>% 
  filter(regulated_by_methylation)

nonmethdepCT <-CT_genes %>% 
  filter(!regulated_by_methylation)

table(CT_genes$group, CT_genes$CpG_promoter)
##              
##               high intermediate low
##   MethDep       25           61  22
##   Non-MethDep   19            7  11
# table(methdepCT$CpG_promoter)/dim(methdepCT)[1]
# table(nonmethdepCT$CpG_promoter)/dim(nonmethdepCT)[1]

Proportionnally, Non-MethDep CT genes show more high CpG density promoters than MethDep CT genes, that have more intermediate density promoters. This is actually quite logical as in female, the MethDep are methylated and thus at risk of being mutated during evolution and lose CpG Islands, whereas non Methdep kept them.

Let’s have a look at the distribution of the promoters CpG density in both groups.

# summary(methdepCT$CpG_density)
# summary(nonmethdepCT$CpG_density)

CT_genes %>% 
  filter(!is.na(regulated_by_methylation)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = CpG_density, 
             fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outliers = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = MethDep_colors) +
  theme_bw() +
  ylab("CpG density of promoters (%)") +
  xlab("CG genes") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        aspect.ratio = 2)

Boxplot show that there is more variance for Non-MethDep genes. Is there a statistically significant difference ?

First I have to check the data normality to know what test to do.

shapiro.test(methdepCT$CpG_density)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  methdepCT$CpG_density
## W = 0.94553, p-value = 0.0002389
shapiro.test(nonmethdepCT$CpG_density)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  nonmethdepCT$CpG_density
## W = 0.93521, p-value = 0.03255

p value is significative for both so we reject normality of the data

Use a Wilcoxon test to compare distributions as they are not normal and few observations.

wilcox.test(methdepCT$CpG_density, nonmethdepCT$CpG_density)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  methdepCT$CpG_density and nonmethdepCT$CpG_density
## W = 1620.5, p-value = 0.08719
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

The pvalue testing the difference between the distributions is not significative, we can’t say that there’s a difference between those two distributions. There’s then no statistically significative difference between those two distributions and the CpG density of promoters that are MethDep and Non-MethDep.

Review 3.4

It may be interesting to investigate the evolutionary track of these CG genes, particularly the X-linked Methdep ones, as they tend to be organized as family gene clusters. How much are they conserved, are they primate/hominoid-specific ?

Question is then, how much are the X-linked MethDep CT conserved through evolution? For that, I need to find the tools to be able to compare MethDep and non MethDep and see if MethDep are more conserved before the others, if some are more recent. I need different species that recapitulate evolution.

Those are the genes I analyse and the species I’m using.

gene_names <- all_genes$external_gene_name

all_genes <- all_genes %>% 
  mutate(group = case_when(CT_gene_type == "CT_gene" & regulated_by_methylation & X_linked ~ "X-linked Methdep CG",
                           CT_gene_type == "CT_gene" & regulated_by_methylation & !X_linked ~ "Not X Methdep CG",
                           CT_gene_type == "CT_gene" & !regulated_by_methylation ~ "Non-Methdep CG",
                           CT_gene_type == "other" & X_linked ~ "X-linked other",
                           CT_gene_type == "other" & !X_linked & chr != "Y" ~ "Autosomal other"))

table(all_genes$group, useNA = "ifany")
## 
##     Autosomal other      Non-Methdep CG    Not X Methdep CG X-linked Methdep CG 
##               23247                  37                  39                  69 
##      X-linked other                <NA> 
##                 886                 210
n_in_group <- table(all_genes$group, useNA = "ifany") %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  dplyr::rename("group" = "Var1", "n_in_group" = "Freq")

species <- c("mmusculus",  # mouse
             "mmulatta",   # macaque
             "ggorilla", # gorilla
             "ptroglodytes", # chimp
             "clfamiliaris",  # dog
             "ggallus",    # chicken
             "drerio",      # zebrafish
             "dmelanogaster", # drosophilia
             "xtropicalis", # Xenope frog
             "celegans") # worm
species
##  [1] "mmusculus"     "mmulatta"      "ggorilla"      "ptroglodytes" 
##  [5] "clfamiliaris"  "ggallus"       "drerio"        "dmelanogaster"
##  [9] "xtropicalis"   "celegans"

Ensembl database has information about orthologs and evolution, I can access and manipulate those using BiomaRt.

ensembl <- useMart("ensembl", dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl")

# To see what I want to get from ensembl, see here
# View(listAttributes(ensembl))
# I chose the attributes I wanted there

# I want a table per specie

for (specie in species) {
  attributes <- c("external_gene_name", "ensembl_gene_id",
                  paste0(specie, "_homolog_ensembl_gene"), # gene stable id
                  paste0(specie, "_homolog_associated_gene_name"), # gene name
                  paste0(specie, "_homolog_subtype"), # last common ancestor
                  paste0(specie, "_homolog_orthology_type"), # homology type
                  paste0(specie, "_homolog_perc_id"), # %id. target species gene identical to query gene
                  paste0(specie, "_homolog_orthology_confidence")) # orthology confidence [0 low, 1 high]
  
  tmp <-  getBM(attributes = attributes,
                filters = "external_gene_name",
                values = gene_names,
                mart = ensembl)
  
colnames(tmp) <- c("external_gene_name", "ensembl_gene_id",
                  "homolog_ensembl_gene","homolog_associated_gene_name", 
                  "homolog_subtype", "homolog_orthology_type", "homolog_perc_id",
                  "homolog_orthology_confidence")
  tmp <- tmp %>% 
    filter(!is.na(homolog_perc_id)) %>% # to keep only when ortholog found
    mutate(species = specie)
  assign(paste0(specie, "_orthologs"), tmp)
}

What does these data look like ? Example with the mouse here.

mmusculus_orthologs

All genes can be represented numerous times as they can have a multitude of orthologs, with more or less confidence and identity. Here are the number of genes for which there is at least one ortholog and the number of genes that have confident orthologs.

mmusculus_orthologs %>% 
  pull(external_gene_name) %>% 
  unique() %>% 
  length()
## [1] 17511
mmusculus_orthologs %>% 
  filter(homolog_orthology_confidence == 1) %>% 
  filter(!duplicated(external_gene_name)) %>% 
  nrow()
## [1] 16419

In order to visualise those results and compare species, I want to know what percentage of each group of genes has orthologs in each specie.

species_data <- list(mmusculus_orthologs, mmulatta_orthologs, ggorilla_orthologs,
                     ptroglodytes_orthologs,clfamiliaris_orthologs,
                     ggallus_orthologs, drerio_orthologs, dmelanogaster_orthologs,
                     xtropicalis_orthologs, celegans_orthologs)

# I want a table with one line per gene found in each specie
all_orthologs <- tibble()

for (i in 1:length(species_data)) {
  # First I want to make sure I'm keeping a confident one where there is 
  tmp1 <- species_data[[i]] %>% 
    group_by(external_gene_name) %>%
    filter(homolog_orthology_confidence == "1") %>% # keeps the confident one if there is one
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!duplicated(external_gene_name)) # keeps only one if same %
  
  # Then I keep the max % when it's not confident 
  # (when just doing this, the duplicated filter was removing confident ones)
  tmp2 <- species_data[[i]] %>% 
    filter(!external_gene_name %in% tmp1$external_gene_name) %>% 
    group_by(external_gene_name) %>%
    filter(homolog_perc_id == max(homolog_perc_id)) %>% # keeps the more alike
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!duplicated(external_gene_name))
  
  tmp <- rbind(tmp1, tmp2)  
  
  all_orthologs <- rbind(all_orthologs, tmp)
}

all_orthologs

The table here contains one line per gene in each specie, either the high confidence one or the maximum percentage of id.

all_orthologs_total_n <- all_orthologs %>% 
  left_join(dplyr::select(all_genes, external_gene_name, group)) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(group)) %>% 
  group_by(species, group) %>% 
  summarise(n_total_in_specie = n())

all_orthologs_highconf_n <- all_orthologs %>% 
  filter(homolog_orthology_confidence == "1") %>% 
  left_join(dplyr::select(all_genes, external_gene_name, group)) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(group)) %>% 
  group_by(species, group) %>% 
  summarise(n_highconf_in_specie = n())

all_orthologs_lowconf_n <- all_orthologs %>% 
  filter(homolog_orthology_confidence == "0") %>% 
  left_join(dplyr::select(all_genes, external_gene_name, group)) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(group)) %>% 
  group_by(species, group) %>% 
  summarise(n_lowconf_in_specie = n())

all_orthologs_perc <- all_orthologs_total_n %>% 
  left_join(all_orthologs_highconf_n) %>% 
  left_join(all_orthologs_lowconf_n) %>% 
  left_join(n_in_group) %>% 
  mutate(total_percentage_in_specie = n_total_in_specie/n_in_group * 100,
         highconf_percentage_in_specie = n_highconf_in_specie/n_in_group * 100,
         lowconf_percentage_in_specie = n_lowconf_in_specie/n_in_group * 100) %>% 
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("Autosomal other", "X-linked other", 
                                          "Non-Methdep CG", "Not X Methdep CG", 
                                          "X-linked Methdep CG"))) %>% 
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = c("ptroglodytes", "mmulatta", "ggorilla", 
                                              "clfamiliaris", "mmusculus",
                                              "ggallus", "xtropicalis", "drerio",
                                              "dmelanogaster", "celegans")))

all_orthologs_perc

I can use this table to do a visualisation.

all_orthologs_perc %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = total_percentage_in_specie, y = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(aes(x = 100), fill = "white", color = "grey47", alpha = 0.3)+
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = all_groups_colors) +
  facet_grid(~species) +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylab("Genes") +
  xlab("Percentage of conservated genes") + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        aspect.ratio = 1.5,
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, 
                                   size = 7, 
                                   vjust = 3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 50, 100))

We can see that, for mmusculus, X-linked CG genes are way less conserved than all others X-linked. MethDep CT genes seems to be quite specific to primates.

Review 3.5

And for the ones that are present in the mouse genome, it would be interesting to assess whether there is conservation of their male-specific expression in germ cells (versus female germ cells) and female-specific expression in embryos (versus male embryos).

Question is then, is it conserved in mouse to have male specificity? This could hint towards mice study. This has to be looked at in pre implanted embryo and in gametogenesis, to have a comparative analysis between male and female.

The answers found at the previous question, showing there isn’t really a conservation of those genes in the mice as the sex biased genes are mostly human specific. Other elements of answer are more detailed in Axelle’s review
